title: The mole, molar mass and simple stoichiometry
blurb: Calculate molar mass, convert between grams, moles and particles by hand, and use a balanced equation's mole ratio to find how much product forms.
question: Methane burns as CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O. Using C = 12.0, H = 1.0 and O = 16.0, how many grams of CO₂ form when 8.0 g of methane burns completely?

teach.h: The mole is a counting unit
teach.body: Formally, one mole is 6.02 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, ions or formula units): Avogadro's number. In plain English: a mole is a chemist's 'dozen', just a far bigger number, because atoms are so small. One mole of water is 6.02 × 10²³ water molecules; one mole of NaCl is 6.02 × 10²³ formula units. Moles let you count particles by weighing them.

items.label: mass of 1 mol of H₂O (H 1.0, O 16.0)

teach.caption: Atomic masses are always given in the item (for example C = 12.0, O = 16.0). Use exactly the values given.

teach.h: Molar mass: add up the formula
teach.body: Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in g/mol. Add the atomic mass of every atom in the formula, multiplying by each subscript and by everything inside parentheses. It equals the formula mass in amu: one water molecule is 18.0 amu, and one mole of water is 18.0 g.

A balanced equation's coefficients are mole ratios. In N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, 1 mol of N₂ reacts with 3 mol of H₂ to make 2 mol of NH₃. Subscripts and masses do not give the ratio. So 6.0 mol of NH₃ needs 6.0 × 3/2 = 9.0 mol of H₂. The reactant that runs out first (the limiting reactant) sets how much product can form.

teach.h: Grams of A to grams of B
teach.caption: Never jump from grams of A straight to grams of B: always pass through moles and the coefficient ratio.

teach.h: Scenario: Tomás and the water molecules
teach.body: Tomás, a pre-nursing student, is asked how many molecules are in 9.0 g of water (H 1.0, O 16.0). Molar mass = 18.0 g/mol. Moles = 9.0 ÷ 18.0 = 0.50 mol. Molecules = 0.50 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³. He checks the size: half a mole should be half of Avogadro's number, and it is.

Percent by mass of an element = (mass of that element in 1 mol ÷ molar mass) × 100. Oxygen in water: 16.0 ÷ 18.0 × 100 = 88.9%. Carbon in CO₂: 12.0 ÷ 44.0 × 100 = 27.3%. Use masses, not atom counts: carbon is 1 of 3 atoms in CO₂ but only 27.3% of the mass.

teach.text: Moles = grams ÷ molar mass (dividing, not multiplying). Multiply by subscripts and through parentheses when finding molar mass. Take mole ratios from COEFFICIENTS, never from subscripts or masses. Avogadro's number counts particles per mole, not per gram. And 22.4 L per mole applies only to a gas at 0 °C and 1 atm, when the item gives it.

items: Molar mass (g/mol) = sum of atomic masses × subscripts, using the values given.
Moles = grams ÷ molar mass; grams = moles × molar mass; particles = moles × 6.02 × 10²³.
Mole ratios come from the coefficients of a balanced equation.
Grams A → moles A → moles B → grams B. Percent by mass = element mass ÷ molar mass × 100.

summary: You can now calculate molar mass from a formula, convert between grams, moles and particles by hand, and use a balanced equation's coefficients to find how much product forms or how much reactant is needed. You can also find percent composition by mass.

A.q: What is the molar mass of ammonia, NH₃? (Use N = 14.0, H = 1.0.)

whyNot.0: 15.0 counts only one hydrogen; the subscript 3 means three H atoms.
whyNot.2: 42.0 multiplies nitrogen by 3; the subscript applies to hydrogen only.
whyNot.3: 45.0 multiplies both atoms by 3; only hydrogen has the subscript 3.

A.q: How many particles are in one mole of any substance?
A.why: One mole is Avogadro's number of particles: 6.02 × 10²³.

whyNot.1: A negative exponent would be a tiny fraction; a mole is an enormous count.
whyNot.2: 22.4 L is the volume of one mole of gas at 0 °C and 1 atm, not a particle count.
whyNot.3: Avogadro's number is 6.02 × 10²³, not a round 10²³.

A.q: How many moles are in 36.0 g of water, H₂O? (Use H = 1.0, O = 16.0.)
A.why: Molar mass of H₂O = 18.0 g/mol. Moles = 36.0 ÷ 18.0 = 2.00 mol.

whyNot.0: 0.500 mol divides molar mass by mass (18.0 ÷ 36.0).
whyNot.1: 648 multiplies grams by molar mass; divide instead.
whyNot.3: 3.60 mol moves the decimal point and does not use the molar mass.

B.q: What is the mass of 0.250 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (Use Ca = 40.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0.)

whyNot.0: 17.0 g uses 68.0 g/mol, counting only one oxygen (0.250 × 68.0).
whyNot.1: 400 g divides 100 by 0.250; moles × molar mass gives grams.
whyNot.3: 100 g is the mass of one full mole, not 0.250 mol.

B.q: In 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, how many moles of O₂ react with 5.0 mol of H₂?
B.why: The ratio H₂ : O₂ is 2 : 1, so 5.0 mol H₂ needs 5.0 ÷ 2 = 2.5 mol O₂.

whyNot.0: 10 mol inverts the ratio (5.0 × 2); O₂ is the smaller coefficient.
whyNot.3: 1.0 mol is the coefficient of O₂, not the amount needed for 5.0 mol of H₂.

B.q: Which of these samples contains the most moles? (Use H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0.)
B.why: 36 ÷ 18 = 2.0 mol of H₂O. The others are each 1.0 mol: 44 ÷ 44, 32 ÷ 32 and 18 ÷ 18.

whyNot.0: 44 g is the largest mass, but CO₂'s molar mass is 44, so it is 1.0 mol.
whyNot.1: O₂'s molar mass is 32, so 32 g is 1.0 mol.
whyNot.2: 18 g of water is 1.0 mol, half the moles in 36 g.

C.q: For CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, how many grams of H₂O form from 16.0 g of CH₄? (Use C = 12.0, H = 1.0, O = 16.0.)
C.why: 16.0 g CH₄ ÷ 16.0 g/mol = 1.00 mol. Ratio CH₄ : H₂O = 1 : 2, so 2.00 mol H₂O × 18.0 g/mol = 36.0 g.

whyNot.0: 18.0 g is one mole of water; the ratio gives two moles of water per mole of methane.
whyNot.1: 16.0 g carries the grams of methane straight across; convert through moles.
whyNot.3: 72.0 g uses 4 mol of water, doubling the ratio twice.

C.q: What is the percent by mass of oxygen in water, H₂O? (Use H = 1.0, O = 16.0.)
C.why: Oxygen supplies 16.0 g of the 18.0 g/mol: 16.0 ÷ 18.0 × 100 = 88.9%.

whyNot.0: 33.3% counts atoms (1 of 3) instead of mass.
whyNot.3: 50.0% treats hydrogen and oxygen as equal shares.

C.q: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, 2.0 mol of N₂ is mixed with 3.0 mol of H₂. How many moles of NH₃ can form?
C.why: 2.0 mol N₂ would need 6.0 mol H₂, but only 3.0 mol is present, so H₂ is limiting. 3.0 mol H₂ × (2 ÷ 3) = 2.0 mol NH₃.

whyNot.0: 4.0 mol uses the N₂ amount, but there is not enough H₂ to react with all of it.
whyNot.2: 3.0 mol assumes a 1:1 ratio between H₂ and NH₃; the ratio is 3 : 2.
whyNot.3: 6.0 mol is the H₂ that 2.0 mol of N₂ would need, not the product formed.

reteach.title: Buying eggs by the dozen
reteach.question: If eggs came only in cartons of a dozen, how would you count 60 eggs, and how does that match the mole?

blocks.body: 60 eggs is 5 dozen: you divide the count by 12. A mole works the same way, with 6.02 × 10²³ in each 'carton'. And if you know one carton of eggs weighs 600 g, a 1,800 g pile must be 3 cartons. That is grams ÷ molar mass = moles. A recipe that says '2 eggs for every 1 cup of flour' is a mole ratio: it compares cartons (moles), not weights.

blocks.text: A recipe ratio counts items, not weights. In chemistry, compare moles using coefficients; never compare grams directly.

explain.body: A mole is 6.02 × 10²³ particles. Particles = moles × 6.02 × 10²³; moles = particles ÷ 6.02 × 10²³.

test.q: How many atoms are in 3.0 mol of helium?

whyNot.0: 2.01 × 10²³ divides Avogadro's number by 3 instead of multiplying.
whyNot.3: 3.0 × 10²³ drops Avogadro's 6.02 and just attaches the exponent.

explain.body: Add the atomic masses of every atom, multiplying by subscripts and through parentheses. The result is in g/mol.

test.q: What is the molar mass of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄? (Use H = 1.0, S = 32.0, O = 16.0.)

whyNot.0: 49.0 counts one of each atom (1 + 32 + 16); apply the subscripts.
whyNot.2: 50.0 counts two H but only one O; oxygen has the subscript 4.
whyNot.3: 97.0 counts only one hydrogen; the subscript 2 gives two H atoms.

explain.body: Moles = grams ÷ molar mass. Grams = moles × molar mass. Check the size: less than one molar mass of material means less than one mole.

test.q: How many moles are in 64.0 g of oxygen gas, O₂? (Use O = 16.0.)
test.why: Molar mass of O₂ = 32.0 g/mol. 64.0 ÷ 32.0 = 2.00 mol.

whyNot.0: 4.00 mol uses 16.0 g/mol, the mass of a single O atom; oxygen gas is O₂.
whyNot.1: 0.500 mol divides 32.0 by 64.0; moles = grams ÷ molar mass.
whyNot.3: 1.00 mol would be 32.0 g, half this sample.

explain.body: Coefficients are mole ratios. To go from one substance to another, multiply moles of the known by (coefficient of wanted ÷ coefficient of known).

test.q: In 2 KClO₃ → 2 KCl + 3 O₂, how many moles of O₂ form from 4.0 mol of KClO₃?

whyNot.1: 3.0 mol is the coefficient of O₂, not the amount from 4.0 mol of KClO₃.
